title: Optimizing LLM Serving Efficiency: Moving Beyond KV Cache Reuse to Token-Load Awareness with Ray Serve LLM | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale (with NVIDIA's Dynamo team) argues that maximizing KV cache reuse is the wrong routing objective for LLM serving fleets: their token-load-aware KVAwareRouter in Ray Serve LLM deliberately sacrifices some cache hit rate for balanced token load, beating cache-affinity and consistent-hashing routers on p99 latency, TTFT, TPOT and throughput in async RL rollouts and replayed Claude Code agent traces.

themes.theme: Why LLM routing breaks microservice assumptions

insights.claim: LLM request routing is fundamentally harder than traditional microservice load balancing because inference is stateful (KV cache reuse across requests), highly heterogeneous in sequence lengths, and non-deterministic in output length, making per-request cost unpredictable at admission time.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: The orchestration/routing layer is becoming a distinct value layer in AI infra — differentiation is moving above the inference engine, favoring platforms like Anyscale/Ray and NVIDIA Dynamo.

insights.claim: The routing decision of which vLLM replica gets the next request directly determines TTFT, TPOT, and throughput at fleet scale, making the router one of the highest-leverage components in LLM serving economics.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Serving-cost efficiency gains increasingly come from scheduling software, not just GPUs — watch inference-orchestration vendors as a margin lever for AI operators.
insights.quote: the most critical decision your router makes is simple: Who gets the next request?

insights.claim: Optimizing purely for KV cache reuse is a misconception in LLM serving: cache overlap only measures prefill work saved, not the work an engine still has to do, so it should serve as an input to load estimation rather than the routing objective itself.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Challenges the prevailing prefix-caching-first orthodoxy in inference stacks; vendors selling pure cache-affinity routing may be optimizing the wrong metric for heterogeneous workloads.
insights.quote: KV cache affinity is still important, but its role changes: it is a proxy for load estimation, not the routing objective itself.
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More

insights.claim: Pure KV cache affinity routing causes 'request herding': once one replica caches a shared prefix like a system prompt, requests from many unrelated conversations preferentially collide on that replica, creating severe token load imbalance.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: A named failure mode for cache-greedy inference schedulers — relevant diligence question for any inference-optimization startup claiming cache-hit-rate wins.

insights.claim: Consistent-hashing session affinity balances the number of sessions per replica but not the actual compute, because sessions vary wildly in length; multiple long-running straggler sessions can land on one replica despite an even session distribution.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Request-count load balancing metrics are misleading for LLM fleets; utilization claims based on them should be discounted.
insights.quote: request-level balance does not guarantee actual load balance

insights.claim: Ray Serve LLM's KVAwareRouter scores replicas on a single 'token load' metric combining remaining prefill load (uncached incoming tokens plus active prefill) and ongoing decode load, capturing both compute-bound and memory-bound work per replica.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for evaluating inference schedulers: does the router estimate remaining work, or just cache overlap and request counts?
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More

insights.claim: In an asynchronous multi-turn RL rollout benchmark (8 rollouts x 10 turns, 2K-token inputs, 1K tokens per turn with two 8K-token stragglers, concurrency 16), KVAwareRouter achieved the best p99 end-to-end rollout latency despite a lower prefix cache hit rate than pure cache-affinity or consistent-hash routers.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: RL post-training (rollout generation) is emerging as a distinct serving workload class; routing gains there directly compress RL training step time and cost.
insights.locator: Why Isn't Maximizing KV Cache Reuse Alone Enough?

insights.claim: KVAwareRouter removes the need for client-supplied session IDs by discovering KV cache overlap automatically from engine-emitted cache events, and scales via replicated routers that share load updates asynchronously under an eventually consistent view.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Lowers integration friction versus session-affinity schemes — an adoption advantage for Ray Serve LLM in multi-tenant serving platforms.

insights.claim: Session affinity via consistent hashing still wins in three regimes: when cache misses are very expensive (long multi-turn chats), when cross-session cache reuse is limited beyond a shared system prompt, and when sessions have similar workloads — token-load-aware routing requires coefficient tuning to beat it.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: No single routing policy dominates; configurable, workload-specific routing is the product thesis — favors platforms over point solutions.

themes.theme: Claude Code traces as the benchmark workload

insights.claim: Coding agents are now one of the most popular LLM inference workloads, and their traffic shape is extreme: heavy-tailed session lifetimes where some sessions span dozens of turns and accumulate millions of input tokens while others are single-turn.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Agentic coding traffic is reshaping inference infra requirements (long contexts, session heterogeneity) — a demand signal for KV-cache-tiering, long-context hardware, and serving-layer vendors.
insights.quote: Coding agents are one of the most popular LLM inference workloads today
insights.locator: Case Study: Replaying Claude Code Traces

insights.claim: Replaying the Weka Claude Code trace corpus against gpt-oss-120b, KVAwareRouter beat session-affinity consistent hashing on TTFT, TPOT, and throughput by trading some prefix cache hit rate for lower per-replica decode-load variance.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Real-world agent traces, not synthetic benchmarks, are becoming the credibility bar for inference performance claims — expect trace-replay benchmarking to spread across vendors.
insights.locator: Ray Serve LLM's KVAwareRouter considers both

insights.claim: Prefix cache hit rate degrades as concurrency rises because KV cache eviction invalidates the router's assumptions, meaning cache-reuse benefits shrink exactly when clusters are busiest.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Supports the case for KV cache offloading/external memory tiers (a growing infra niche) since GPU-resident cache alone loses value under load.
insights.quote: prefix cache hit rate drops as concurrency increases, highlighting the impact of KV cache eviction

themes.theme: NVIDIA Dynamo collaboration and ecosystem positioning

insights.claim: Anyscale and NVIDIA's Dynamo team integrated Dynamo's KV indexer and request-scoring modules into Ray Serve LLM through modular interfaces, keeping event, request, and data planes Ray-native while Dynamo computes KV cache overlap for replica scoring.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is pushing Dynamo as embeddable inference-infrastructure middleware inside third-party stacks — extending its moat from silicon into the serving software layer.

insights.claim: Non-deterministic output length is an unsolved industry-wide routing problem: requests admitted as lightweight can develop long decode phases and collide on one replica, and one proposed fix is for agentic harnesses to pass hints about expected generation behavior to the router.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Points to a coming interface between agent frameworks and serving layers (generation-length hints) — a standardization opportunity to watch.
insights.quote: Accurately accounting for this uncertainty remains an open challenge across the industry.

insights.claim: Anyscale plans to extend KVAwareRouter to prefill-decode disaggregated deployments, data-parallel deployments, and multimodal workloads, signaling that disaggregated serving is the next battleground for routing policy.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang
insights.so_what: Prefill/decode disaggregation is consolidating as the default large-scale serving architecture; infra bets should assume routing and scheduling complexity keeps rising.
insights.locator: In the near future, we plan
